newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-SSAB Q1 profit seen indicating strong 1997.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-SSAB Q1 profit seen indicating strong 1997.

text.p: Swedish steel group SSAB reported lower first quarter profits on Thursday but raised expectations for the rest of the year by saying it may increase prices in local currencies in the second quarter.
"It looks positive for developments during the rest of the year," Goran Villner, analyst at Aros Securities, told Reuters.
SSAB's first quarter profit after financial items fell 44 percent to 470 million crowns ($61.4 million), right on target according to a Reuter poll of analysts' forecasts.
Sales fell to 4.33 billion crowns from 4.70 billion and earnings per share dipped to 2.60 crowns from 4.70.
Analysts welcomed the operating profit of 437 million crowns, down from 751 million crowns a year earlier.
"Profit after financial items was in line with expectations but operating profit was 100 million crowns higher and net financial items fell more than expected," an analyst said.
"This is positive as operations are key and the profit is very good," the analyst added. Net financial items fell to 33 million crowns from 93 million.
Relief that earnings were in line with expectations along with the brighter second quarter outlook cheered market players and SSAB shares jumped 10 crowns to close at 142 crowns.

Profits were hurt by steel prices being 10 percent lower in Swedish crowns during the first quarter compared with the corresponding quarter of 1996 but prices were one percent higher than in the fourth quarter last year, the company said.
"After five quarters with falling prices we can note a small price rise of more than one percent in the first quarter," chief executive Leif Gustafsson said in the results statement.
"This price rise indicates a change in trends. We will be able to raise prices in local currencies somewhat further on most markets in the second quarter," he added.

In 1996, steel consumption within the European Union fell eight percent, putting pressure on prices. But the situation stabilised in the first quarter, although prices were still three percent lower than average 1996 prices.
"Steel demand has now stabilised and during the first quarter there were some price hikes and some price falls on the group's steel products," SSAB said.
But it still did not see tangible signs of more consumption. "Continued price development will be the decisive factor for group earnings in the rest of the year," SSAB said.
